Lake trout (Salvelinus namaycush) embryos develop slowly within demersal eggs deposited over rocky substrates in oligotrophic lakes, with the newly hatched alevin emerging from the chorion at a remarkably small size. Field collections indicate that at the moment of eclosion, the wet weight of a yolk-sac larva is approximately 0.0082 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0082 grams], a value corresponding closely to the theoretical mass calculated from an egg diameter of 2.5 millimeters. This modest initial mass reflects the substantial energy reserves packaged within the yolk, which sustains the endotrophic larva through the period of yolk absorption before the onset of exogenous feeding. During this lecithotrophic phase, the alevin remains largely sedentary within the interstitial spaces of the spawning substrate, gradually depleting its yolk stores as organ systems continue to differentiate. The timing of the transition to active feeding is critical, as larvae that fail to locate suitable prey items shortly after yolk-sac resorption may reach the point of no return, leading to irreversible starvation and mortality.

Sexual maturation in lake trout is tightly linked to body size rather than age alone, with puberty typically initiated once individuals attain a total length of approximately 46 centimeters [Lp = approximately 46 centimeters]. Field surveys and mark-recapture studies have documented that this threshold length can vary somewhat among populations, with a reported range of 42 to 50 centimeters [Lp = 42 to 50 centimeters], likely reflecting differences in local growth rates and thermal regimes. Reaching this size threshold triggers the onset of gametogenesis, as the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis becomes activated, initiating vitellogenesis in females and spermiation in males. The total length at puberty represents a critical life-history switch, as individuals must divert increasing proportions of assimilated energy toward gonad development rather than somatic growth. Populations inhabiting warmer, more productive waters tend to reach this size more quickly than those in ultra-oligotrophic systems, although the thermal constraints on metabolism at colder temperatures often extend the pre-pubertal period considerably.

Reproductive output in lake trout has been quantified under controlled laboratory conditions designed to simulate the species' preferred thermal environment. At a stable water temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], gravid females have been observed to produce an average of approximately 47 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 47 eggs per day] during the peak of the spawning season. This daily fecundity rate, sustained over the relatively brief spawning window characteristic of fall-spawning salmonids, reflects the high energetic investment that iteroparous adults allocate to each reproductive event. The eggs are relatively large compared to those of many other salmonids, a trait that correlates with the substantial yolk reserves needed to support the extended embryonic development period typical of cold-water incubation. After spawning, adults may migrate back to deeper lake regions, though some individuals remain in near-shore areas to recover energy reserves depleted during gamete production. The 10 °C [T = 10 °C] temperature used in these laboratory trials approximates the thermal conditions found in the hypolimnion of deep boreal lakes during the autumn spawning period.

The maximum attainable body size of lake trout has been documented through long-term monitoring programs targeting trophy specimens in large, undisturbed northern water bodies. The ultimate standard length recorded for this species reaches 150 centimeters [Li = 150 centimeters], a formidable size that places Salvelinus namaycush among the largest charr species globally. Corresponding to this extreme length, the ultimate wet weight of the largest individuals has been measured at approximately 32,700 grams [Wwi = approximately 32,700 grams], a mass that is rarely achieved except in systems with abundant prey fish and minimal fishing pressure. Achieving such asymptotic dimensions requires decades of sustained growth, as growth rates decelerate markedly after sexual maturation when surplus energy is increasingly partitioned toward reproduction rather than somatic increase. These giant individuals are most frequently encountered in deep, cold lakes of the Canadian Shield where piscivorous lake trout occupy the apex predator niche and experience low natural mortality. The attainment of such large body sizes also confers reproductive advantages, as fecundity scales positively with female size in this species.

Longevity records for lake trout indicate a remarkably extended lifespan, particularly for individuals inhabiting cold, unproductive northern lakes where metabolic rates are suppressed. The maximum documented lifespan under natural conditions, at a reference temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], is approximately 18,250 days [am = approximately 18,250 days], which corresponds to roughly 50 years. This exceptional longevity is among the highest recorded for any salmonid species and reflects the extremely slow pace of life characteristic of populations occupying the coldest thermal niches. Senescence in lake trout is gradual, with older individuals showing reduced reproductive output and increased susceptibility to disease, though some reproductively viable adults exceeding 40 years of age have been captured in pristine systems. The extended lifespan is ecologically significant because it allows multiple reproductive episodes over several decades, buffering populations against occasional years of poor recruitment. Climate warming poses a direct threat to this life-history strategy, as higher temperatures accelerate metabolic rates and are predicted to reduce both the maximum age and the size at which lake trout can persist in their native habitats.
